Level 3 · Advanced · Week 10

Project Studio 1

Design first: classes, data and milestones – then build the core.

What you will learn

  • Design your project on paper with CRC cards and a class diagram.
  • Plan your milestones: small steps you can finish and save.
  • Start a git repository for your project and make your first commits.
  • Check that every picture, sound or library you use is allowed.

Design first

Builders draw plans before they pour concrete. Programmers design before they type. Your design answers three questions: Which classes do I need? What does each one know and do? Who works with whom?

CRC cards

A CRC card is an index card for one class: the Class name, its Responsibilities (what it knows and does) and its Collaborators (the classes it works with). Here is one from the reference project, Maze Muncher:

Tip: if a card’s responsibility list gets long, that class is doing too much – split it in two.

Class diagrams: “is a” and “has a”

A class diagram shows all the classes and how they connect. An arrow with a hollow triangle means is a (inheritance). A line with a diamond means has a (composition).

Read it aloud: a Game has a Maze, a Player and some Ghosts; a Chaser is a Ghost.

Milestones and save points

Big projects are built in small steps. After each step works, you commit – a save point you can always return to.

A good commit message starts with a verb and says what changed: Add Maze class that loads a grid, Fix player walking through walls. Your project needs 8 or more meaningful commits by the showcase.

Exercise10.4: My repository and first commits

SafetyMay I use this? Licenses

Everything in your project must be yours or allowed. Python’s standard library is free to use, and your own drawings and sounds are yours. For anything made by someone else, look at its license: CC0 = free for anyone; CC BY = free if you give credit; “All rights reserved” or no license = do not use. Never download anything without a parent, and list every borrowed item in the “Credits” part of your README.

Reflect

Which class was hardest to describe? Why?

What will your next commit message be?

New words

CRC card
A card for one class: Class name, Responsibilities, Collaborators.
class diagram
A drawing of classes as boxes, joined by “is a” and “has a” links.
composition
“Has a”: an object is built from other objects (a Game has a Maze).
milestone
A small goal on the way to the finished project.
repository
A project folder that git keeps a history of.
license
The rules that say how you may use someone’s work.

Homework: Project Studio 1

15–20 minutes of project work. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CoreBuild your core (Milestone 2)

Work on your project in Documents/coding-projects/<your project>.

  1. Pick one class from your CRC cards and make its __init__ and one method really work.

  2. Run it. When it works, commit in Terminal:

    git add .
git commit -m "Make Player move one cell"

  3. Repeat for another small step. Aim for 3 or more new commits this week.

Copy your new commit messages from git log --oneline:

ChallengeYour first test

Create test_.py next to your code and write one test for the method you just finished (look at the example in workbook chapter 11). Run it in Thonny with Tools → Open system shell... and python -m pytest -q. Does it pass? Break the code on purpose: does it fail?

CreativeTitle screen

Design the first thing a player sees: the name of your project, the controls, and a picture made with turtle. Use the Okabe–Ito palette and write the controls in text (not color alone). Sketch it here, then code it if you have time.

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true
